> 「以三千大千世界碎为微尘……若是微尘众实有者，佛则不说是微尘众。」……「若世界实有者，即是一合相。……一合相者，即是不可说，但凡夫之人贪著其事。」

Section thirty grinds a world into dust, and then asks what the dust is.

A billion worlds, broken into particles. Are those particles many? Very many — because if the particles were real, the Buddha would not have called them particles.

And the world they came from: if a world were real, it would be 一合相 — a composite, an aggregate.

## 一合相 is the sutra's word for "thing"

A composite: many parts gathered into one apparent whole, sustained for a while, called by a name. Mountains, bodies, institutions, selves.

Everything you can point to is one of these. The word is not pejorative; it is descriptive. Composites exist as composites, which is precisely why they cannot be the ground.

## The particles do not survive either

The obvious move — the one physics makes too — is to say the composite is unreal but the constituents are real.

The sutra closes that exit in the same breath: the particles are also a conventional designation. Break them further and the same logic applies.

The book notes the resonance with the modern result that there is no smallest indivisible unit: every candidate dissolves into relations. The old text arrived at this without instruments, by refusing to let any composite be a ground while refusing to let its parts be one either.

## 不可说 is not a prohibition on speech

The section says the composite is 不可说 — inexpressible.

Not: do not speak of it. The Buddha has just spoken of it for four lines. What is denied is that a concept can correspond to a fixed entity. Words work by boundaries; what they describe has none that hold.

## 贪著其事 — the best phrase in the sutra

And then the closing sentence, which the book singles out: ordinary people 贪著其事 — crave the *matter* of it.

其事. The affair of it. Not the world — the world is not what anyone is greedy for. What is gripped is the layer added on top: my house, my land, my body, my version of how this should go.

This is exact and it is useful. It locates greed not in objects but in the possessive prefix. The composite is neutral; 我的 is the operation.

Which also explains why renunciation so often fails. One can give up objects and keep the prefix, transferring it to the renunciation itself — my practice, my simplicity, my having-given-it-up.

## The test

Take something you own and say what it is without the possessive: not "my flat" but "a flat"; not "my body" but "a body".

Notice the discomfort. That discomfort is not attachment to the object — the object has not changed. It is attachment to 其事, the affair, the small administrative layer where ownership is recorded.

The section does not ask you to give the object up. It asks you to look at the layer.
